posts.author: Diode Holographer
posts.content_md:
Hello there again. 

When last you heard from me I was working on getting an H2 copy from a transmission master. As you may remember I ran out of film before succeeding. Well I just recently got a hold of more film and now I seem to be having a more serious problem.

I believe the problem is in my developer and/or bleach, since they are the only things that have really changed about my system. I'm using PFG-01 film with the JD-2 developer if that info helps.

I ran out of bleach the same time I ran out of film. I made more bleach from chemicals I had previously purchased through a website (using the values given on Holowiki)and I really don't think the bleach is the problem, but I am willing to listen to anyone's thoughts. 

My developer, on the other hand, strikes me as the prime suspect. The part A solution of my developer has gotten quite on the yellow side. Its always had a bit of hue to it, but now its noticabley darker. Nearly the hue of a healthy person's urine. 

When developing a hologram now I can notice no difference in the process. When I put the film in the developer it darkens to a nice density in about 10 to 30 seconds (varying from exposure to exposure) and when I bleach the film it turns clear in about the same time. All of this follows my past experiences, but in the end I get no image. I mean NO image. in the past whenever I did something wrong I usually got at the very least a faint or partial image. Since getting all my supplies back in order I have shot five holograms now and not a single one has shown even the slightest indication of an image.

Is there an easy way to test my developer? Does anyone have any other thoughts as to what the problem might be? Absolutely nothing else about my set up has change.

Looking forward to your responses and thank you for your time and help.

Diode

Since the power output of my laser hasn't changed nor has the distance between my "diverging lens" and the object I can't for the life of me understand why the exposure time would have changed and so greatly. Does the sensetivity of film vary from batch to batch or what could be going on here?

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
The things that effect developer time for me have been time, temperature, dilution and exposure. Check all four. Perhaps the Wiki recipie has an error? 

Film that is fresh and/or pre-treated with water or TEA is much faster than normal film.

It is not my developing time that has changed, its my **exposure** time. 

Now the four things you say to check (time, temperature, dilution and exposure); what do you mean by "time"? Thats a little vague. 

By dilution do you mean my developer? Because I have not diluted the developer at all, it is the same as it has been only darker in color.

By temperature I'm guussing you mean ambient room temperature. That may be different than usual. Can you tell me if the colder the room temp the short the required exposure or visa versa. 

Exposure is the only thing I can see that has changed and it is severly reduced compared to what I was using, but so far thats the only way I've managed to get anything.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
I am hoping someone will pickup the chemistry side of the question as it is not my area of expertise.

> **Colin Kaminski:** The things that effect developer time for me have been time, temperature, dilution and exposure. Check all four. Perhaps the Wiki recipe has an error?

Development time = Longer allows for shorter exposures but creates larger silver crystals and can be noisy.

Temperature = Warmer shortens development time 

Dilution = I don't know how dilution works but clearly more dilution make for longer development time. There may be other effects as well.

Exposure = Longer exposures shorten development times.

An example on how this can be used. if when Lon Moore shot bunch of daises. He kept the room cold to slow down the movement of the flowers. He then used a short exposure time and warm developer. All in an effort to limit the problems of the stability of something living.

So two things could have changed. If you evaporated liquid over time you may have concentrated the developer. More likely the developer is becoming oxidized.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Hey Diode, when a chain has a weak link, the link is replaced. My suggestion, based on the fact that you state the only thing that has changed is your developer and bleach, is to simply make up another batch of dev and bleach. In your mixing, it may be possible that you bleach contaminated your dev, or something elsed contaminated it. Try a new bach of developer first and if you are still having problems, make a new batch of bleach also.

Also, to insure you plates are not fogged or were exposed to light, process one right out of the box. It SHOULD NOT turn dark in the developer straight from the box.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Diode Holographer:** I'm guessing the ammonia odor being given off by my developer (...)

My guess would be your developer has turned bad and far too alkaline.

Try a new developer. With PFG-01 you don't necessarily have to stay with „JD-2“. I believe JD-2 actually is CW-C2, a developer designed for the old Agfa 8E75/8E56 emulsions. It may work OK with PFG-01 but so do a lot of other developers.

My advice would we: buy a commercial developer like D-19, D-8 etc. Or make a simple ascorbic acid developer, maybe one like this:

ascorbic acid....................15g

sodium carbonate.............60g

water...................................1L

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
If you have undeveloped scraps of both batches of film, your old and suspected higher sensitivity newer, check to see if they are of similar cyan color. Agfa plates were all over the place with sensitivity from batch to batch. There was one batch of plates that looked much darker than others while they were being exposed on the object, and I did a d-log e sensitometric test on it this batch needed 1/3 the light to get to the same density as the previous batch. Placing them on a white card along with plates from other batches showed that they were definitely more cyan colored than the others, ostensibly because there was more sensitizing dye in them. I figured that it might have been a scenario worthy of the Three Stooges back at the plant, like "Did I forget to put the dye in? Maybe I'd better put some more in just in case I didn't!"

The holograms came out just as good as any others, and that 3 times sensitivity was a nice improvement! I wonder if there ever was any test program of how much dye to put in emulsions and still get decent single beam reflections?

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
There is a great range of exposures that will reveal an image with most systems. An over exposed hologram will be dimmer than a properly exposed hologram. So will an under exposed hologram! I have found no way to tell the difference with only the hologram in hand and no lab notes.

I have found PFG-01 to be very forgiving and simply by watching it go through the steps with no clock I can get very bright results. You start to get a feel for how dark you want it to go how quickly and how fast you want it to turn clear in the bleach. Exposure tests are a great thing to practice with.
